legal_system: mixed (Palestinian civil administration and Israeli military administration under the Oslo Accords II territorial division)
service_provider: Palestinian Water Authority (PWA); Joint Service Councils (JSCs) and Village Representatives (VRs) at the local level; GVC (Italian NGO) and UNICEF as programme implementer/funder
regulatory_model: Oslo Accords II territorial division (Area A: Palestinian Authority control; Area B: joint Palestinian civil/Israeli security control; Area C: full Israeli control) constraining formal water-infrastructure construction; multilevel humanitarian-development water-trucking governance system embedding trucked-water subsidies into PWA structures
population: rural Bedouin and other communities in Area C unconnected or underserved by the piped water network
sample_size: not_applicable (practice paper documenting programme design/implementation, drawing on OCHA/GVC administrative and needs-assessment data)
effect_measure: descriptive_administrative_and_needs_assessment_statistics
effect_estimate: Approximately 270,000 Palestinians in Area C have inadequate WASH access (OCHA HNO 2017); about 153,000 are unconnected to the water network (GVC et al. 2017); the most vulnerable 11,000 Palestinians (60 communities) pay approximately $6/m3 for private-vendor trucked water, up to NIS 50/m3 (~$15) in remote areas -- roughly 10 times the public rate paid by Areas A/B residents -- and are unable to reach the international minimum standard of 100 l/capita/day (OCHA HRP 2016). The subsidy programme, established 2014, had reached 35,000 people by 2022.
extraction_sample_size: 11,000-270,000 Palestinians across 60+ communities in Area C (official UN/GVC administrative statistics, not a primary survey by these authors)
study_design: doctrinal/institutional practice case study of a humanitarian-development governance mechanism
source_document: Cesari et al. 2022, Waterlines 41(1)
figure: Figure 1

extraction_note: Practice paper documenting the GVC/UNICEF water-trucking subsidy programme (established 2014) in Oslo Accord-defined Area C of the West Bank. Directly examines how Israeli military zoning/occupation law (Area C status, infrastructure demolition risk) forecloses formal piped connection for Palestinian communities, and how the Palestinian Water Authority's humanitarian-development response embeds explicit programme ELIGIBILITY criteria (consumption/price thresholds) into a multilevel governance mechanism. citation: Nijhawan A, Howard G, Poudel M, Pregnolato M, Lo YTE, Ghimire A, Baidya M, Geremew A, Flint A, Mulugeta Y (2022). Assessing the Climate Resilience of Community-Managed Water Supplies in Ethiopia and Nepal. Water 14(8), 1293.
subnational_unit: Kersa and Haramaya districts, Ethiopia; Chitwan and Kaski districts, Nepal
legal_system: Ethiopia: civil_law (federal constitutional); Nepal: civil_law (federal constitutional, post-2015 federalization)
service_provider: community-managed WASH committees / Water Users and Sanitation Committees (WUSCs); local/provincial government (post-federalization, Nepal); woreda (district) offices, Ethiopia
regulatory_model: Nepal's federal drinking water policy requiring user-group financial contribution (20-30% of project construction cost); post-2015 federalization shifting water-supply oversight from federal to provincial/local government in Nepal; Ethiopia's woreda-level administrative support to community WASH committees
population: rural households served by community-managed water supplies (public taps, handpumps, piped systems)
sample_size: 20 rural communities in Ethiopia (Kersa, Haramaya districts, serving 80-500 households each); 15 rural/small-town communities in Nepal (Chitwan, Kaski districts, serving 10-8,500 households each)
effect_measure: embedded_qualitative_case_finding_within_a_resilience_scoring_framework
effect_estimate: In one documented Nepal community, the municipal piped-water supply was recently expanded but 'the user tariff and cost of setting up a new connection are not affordable for several residents who continue to rely on' unsafe boreholes near flood-prone pit latrines. Nepal's federal drinking water policy requires user groups to contribute 20-30% of project construction cost. Only 13% (Ethiopia) and 18% (Nepal) of the national population have access to safely managed drinking water (JMP data cited by the study). Institutional-support and community-governance domain resilience scores (1-5 scale) were the lowest-scoring domains in both countries (HTIW framework, not a household-level access metric).
extraction_sample_size: 20 communities (Ethiopia) + 15 communities (Nepal); affordability finding drawn from community discussions in one specific Nepal site
model_type: qualitative/mixed-methods longitudinal field study applying a structured resilience-scoring framework (How Tough is WASH, HTIW) plus community discussions and key-informant interviews
source_document: Nijhawan et al. 2022, Water 14(8), 1293
figure: Figure 2
section: 3.2 System Scores and High Priority Supplies; 3.3 Systemic Issues of Low Resilience
exact_location: p.12: 'the municipal piped-water supply was recently expanded to this community but the user tariff and cost of setting up a new connection are not affordable for several residents who continue to rely on the boreholes' (BURDEN/economic_access -- a real documented instance of unaffordability blocking a formal connection despite physical service availability). p.13: 'since the federal drinking water policy in Nepal requires user groups to contribute financially toward the cost of construction of the water supply (generally, 20-30% of the project cost), including climate adaptations in projects can be cost prohibitive for communities' and 'federalization has led to confusion about guidelines and the role of officials at different levels of government' (institutional_fragmentation). p.11-12: an Ethiopian school board and kebele (smallest administrative unit) selected a WASH committee 'after discussions... Local residents were not included in this process and have no way to engage with the committee' (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION/participation gap).
extraction_note: Longitudinal mixed-methods field study (Nov 2019-Aug 2021; 20 Ethiopian and 15 Nepali rural/small-town communities) whose central purpose is validating the 'How Tough is WASH' climate-resilience assessment framework across six domains (environment, infrastructure, management, institutional support, community governance, supply chains). The primary reported outcome is a 1-5 resilience score per domain, not a household-level access metric -- included because the field findings embed a specific, real, sourced BURDEN mechanism (Nepal's federal 20-30% user-group cost-sharing policy making a new connection to an already-expanded municipal supply unaffordable for several documented households) and a DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION/participation gap (Ethiopian WASH committee selection excluding resident input). Not quantitative-synthesis-eligible: the affordability finding is a qualitative case example embedded in a resilience-scoring study, not a calculable household-level effect estimate. record_id R072D7FD1C80E. risk_of_bias_rating deferred per RISK_OF_BIAS.md.

citation: Thapa D, Farid MN, Prevost C (2022). Governance drivers of rural water sustainability: Collaboration in frontline service delivery. Journal of Infrastructure, Policy and Development 6(1), 1380.
subnational_unit: rural villages nationwide (PAMSIMAS project villages, including a detailed case study in Alor District)
service_provider: community-managed water user groups (KPSPAM) established under PAMSIMAS (Program for Community-Based Water Supply and Sanitation, Program Air Minum dan Sanitasi Berbasis Masyarakat), with village-authority (frontline government) support
regulatory_model: World Bank/Government of Indonesia community-driven-development rural water program; state embeddedness/frontline collaboration between village authorities and community water user groups rather than a fixed regulatory statute
population: rural villages and their water-point beneficiary households
sample_size: 10-year panel (2008-2018) of PAMSIMAS village water-point functionality monitoring data, plus in-depth qualitative case studies of positive/negative deviant villages
effect_measure: poisson_regression_proportion_ratio
effect_estimate: Poisson regression (Table 1): for every 10-fold increase in village economic conditions (per capita income proxy, log scale), the proportion of fully-functional villages increases by an estimated coefficient reported as approximately 21 percentage points in the adjusted model (about half of the unadjusted Model 1 effect). Villages with above-median per-capita economic conditions were 1.5 times more likely to be consistently functional 2014-2018. Villages covering more than O&M costs from tariffs (39% of sample) showed reinforcing positive functionality association. A 'fully functional' village produces sufficient water for >80% of beneficiaries; some villages (e.g., in Alor District) were nonfunctional/effectively abandoned for almost a decade.
extraction_sample_size: 10-year (2008-2018) panel of PAMSIMAS village water-point functionality records
adjusted_or_unadjusted: both crude and adjusted proportion ratios reported (Table 1)
covariates: village economic conditions/per-capita income, water source conditions, cost-recovery level, presence of dug wells (proxy for water availability)
model_type: Poisson regression (panel) plus qualitative positive/negative deviance case analysis
study_design: mixed_methods (panel regression + qualitative outlier case studies)
source_document: Thapa, Farid & Prevost 2022, Journal of Infrastructure, Policy and Development 6(1)
table: Table 1 (Crude and adjusted proportion ratio of sustainable villages using Poisson regression)
figure: Figure 1 (Number of villages, fully functional vs. not functional)
exact_location: p.2-3: positive outlier villages had 'collaborative state-community relations' where 'village authorities were willing to mobilize village resources and state facilities to reduce coordination hassles, support community mobilization, and create more effective socialization', giving water user group leaders 'the decision space and resource support to solve operations and maintenance (O&M) problems in real time' (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION/bureaucratic_assistance). Negative outlier villages showed 'a lack of support on the part of village authorities' producing 'ineffective community socialization' and community exit from the shared system. Table 1: Poisson regression of village economic conditions and cost-recovery on functionality proportion.
extraction_note: Mixed-methods World Bank study combining 10-year panel regression (Poisson model, village water-point functionality) with qualitative process-tracing of positive/negative deviant PAMSIMAS villages in Indonesia. Central finding: differences in the QUALITY of community participation -- driven by frontline state-society relations between village authorities (a form of local administrative discretion/accommodation) and water user groups -- explain sustained vs. abandoned community water management beyond what village economic/water conditions alone predict. This is a genuine calculable panel-regression effect estimate (own project monitoring data), making it quantitative-synthesis-eligible. record_id RC41D17900D05 (a duplicate ProQuest record, R346D1BF8F31D, was found and excluded as E08). risk_of_bias_rating deferred per RISK_OF_BIAS.md.

citation: Okolie AM, Nnamani KE, Nwangwu C, Agbo HN, Ike CC (2023). Public procurement law, political economy of the lowest responsive bidding, and the development of the water, sanitation and hygiene sector in Nigeria. Review of African Political Economy 49(174), 550-568.
subnational_unit: national, with documented cases in Benue, Bayelsa, Anambra, and Akwa Ibom states
service_provider: Federal Ministry of Water Resources; state ministries of water resources; RUWASSA (Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Agency, state-level implementing agency)
regulatory_model: Public Procurement Act (PPA) 2007's 'lowest responsive bidding' provision, governing the award of government WASH infrastructure contracts
population: national population lacking WASH access, and specifically communities awaiting WASH infrastructure (e.g., school water/sanitation projects) funded via captured procurement processes
sample_size: not_applicable (doctrinal/political-economy analysis: secondary data, policy appraisal, field observation by authors as UNICEF procurement consultants, documented contract-award case examples)
effect_measure: documented_case_examples_and_national_statistics
effect_estimate: Only 68% of the Nigerian population have access to basic water supply and 19% use improved sanitation facilities (2014-2017 UNICEF evaluation); 47 million people practise open defecation; national diarrhoea prevalence rose from 10.2% (2013) to 12.8% (2018); >70,000 under-five deaths annually linked to diarrhoea; 3,208 cholera-related deaths (1 Jan-3 Oct 2021). Documented procurement-capture cases: a Benue State public procuring entity incurred cost overruns on a WASH project subsequently awarded a total budget of only N2.7 million; a state commissioner's account of WASH contracts worth over N800 million awarded to politically-connected contractors in school WASH projects who were fully paid and then abandoned the projects; similar documented cases in Bayelsa, Anambra, and Akwa Ibom states.
extraction_sample_size: national aggregate statistics (UNICEF/national surveys) plus specific documented procurement cases in 4 states
model_type: not_applicable (doctrinal/political-economy analysis with documented case examples)
source_document: Okolie et al. 2023, Review of African Political Economy 49(174)
section: Introduction; lowest responsive bidding and the development of the WASH sector in Nigeria
exact_location: Section 3: quotes a state commissioner explaining 'contracts worth over N800 million were given to [contractors for] schools. They then abandoned the projects... The government has paid all the contractors in this ministry, so it is the fault of the contractors' -- all contractors named as 'people in government' (ENFORCEMENT/regulatory-capture -- the PPA's lowest-responsive-bidding provision is exploited by politically-connected bidders, with delay/abandonment as the outcome and no effective accountability). Benue State case: cost overrun followed by a subsequent award of only N2.7 million for the same project.
extraction_note: Doctrinal/political-economy analysis (secondary data, policy appraisal, and field observation by the authors as UNICEF procurement consultants) of how Nigeria's Public Procurement Act 2007 'lowest responsive bidding' provision is captured by politically-connected contractors ('dominant social forces') to extract public WASH funds, with documented real cases of contract award, payment, and subsequent project abandonment in Benue, Bayelsa, Anambra, and Akwa Ibom states. This is the ENFORCEMENT-mechanism-failure side of the review's scope: a legal instrument nominally designed to ensure competitive, accountable contracting is shown, through real case evidence, to systematically fail to deliver WASH infrastructure to intended communities. National outcome statistics are secondary UNICEF/government data, not this study's own primary data collection. record_id R7D8E7FB109D4. risk_of_bias_rating deferred per RISK_OF_BIAS.md.

citation: Mallory A, Mdee A, Agol D, Hyde-Smith L, Kiogora D, Riungu J, Parker A (2022). The potential for scaling up container-based sanitation in informal settlements in Kenya. Journal of International Development 34(7), 1347-1361.
subnational_unit: Mukuru informal settlements, Nairobi; Naivasha town, Nakuru County; Garissa town
service_provider: Sanergy and Sanivation (container-based sanitation enterprises); Nairobi Water and Sewerage Company; county governments (Nakuru); national Ministry of Water and Sanitation, NEMA, Ministry of Health, WASREB, Water Services Boards
regulatory_model: Kenya's 2010 Constitution Article 43 (right to reasonable standards of sanitation); overlapping/conflicting 2002 and 2016 Water Acts on sanitation-sector institutional roles; post-2010 decentralization creating 47 county governments with disputed sanitation mandates alongside national Water Services Boards
population: residents of urban informal settlements lacking sewered sanitation
sample_size: ~59 semi-structured interviews/focus groups (utility employees, sanitation-enterprise staff, NGO employees, public health officers, 20 manual pit emptiers, 20 vacuum truck operators, national/county government officials), Jan-Mar 2020 fieldwork, snowball sampling to saturation, NVivo thematic analysis
effect_measure: qualitative_case_evidence_with_descriptive_statistics
effect_estimate: Only 7.6% of the sub-Saharan African urban population is estimated to be connected to sewers (17% for the region's total urban population) (WHO/UNICEF 2020). An estimated 46-54% of Kenya's urban population lives in informal settlements. In 10 years since Kenya's 2010 constitutional right to sanitation (Article 43), only one legal case successfully invoked it in court -- a highways-authority case, not a household/settlement case. Garissa: forcible eviction of 2,000 informal-settlement residents declared unconstitutional, with disconnection from existing water/sanitation services forming part of the claim. Sanergy's CBS subsidy is estimated at ~$19/person/year, expected to fall below $10/person with scale (2,000 more toilets/year for 7 years from a 2017 base of 1,200).
extraction_sample_size: ~59 interviews/focus-group participants; secondary WHO/UNICEF/World Bank statistics for national/regional context
study_design: qualitative case study (semi-structured interviews, focus groups, participant observation, document analysis)
source_document: Mallory et al. 2022, Journal of International Development 34(7)
table: Table 1 (Institutions and responsibilities in sanitation provision in Kenya), Table 2 (Interviewees)
section: 2. Revealing the complex fragmentation of sanitation governance; 2.1 Fragmented governance
exact_location: p.1351-1352: 'A new constitution for Kenya was agreed upon in 2010... The right of sanitation in article 43 states that "Every person has the right to accessible and adequate housing, and to reasonable standards of sanitation"... in 10 years, there was only one legal case where the right to sanitation was successfully raised in court' -- a highways-authority case, not one involving informal-settlement households (ELIGIBILITY/judicial_review gap). 'In the case of Garissa... evictions of 2000 informal settlement residents... the forcible eviction of residents was declared unconstitutional, and the right to water and sanitation formed part of the case as residents had been disconnected from their existing services' (judicial_review/disconnection). County governments dispute the 2016 Water Act's alignment with constitutional reforms and continue applying the 2002 Water Act instead (institutional_fragmentation).
extraction_note: Qualitative political-economy case study (Jan-Mar 2020 fieldwork, ~59 interviewees) of two container-based sanitation enterprises in Kenyan informal settlements, examining fragmented governance (overlapping 2002/2016 Water Acts, disputed national/county mandates), a constitutional ELIGIBILITY/enforcement gap (Kenya's Article 43 sanitation right invoked successfully only once in 10 years, and not for informal-settlement households specifically), and a documented judicial_review/disconnection case (Garissa eviction of 2,000 residents declared unconstitutional, disconnection from services part of the claim). Not quantitative-synthesis-eligible: findings are qualitative case evidence and secondary regional/national statistics, not this study's own primary calculable effect estimate. record_id R6D20561D1166. risk_of_bias_rating deferred per RISK_OF_BIAS.md.

citation: Narzetti DA, Marques RC (2022). Policies and incentives for developing universal access to water and sanitation for vulnerable families. Water Policy 24(3), 485-497.
subnational_unit: national, with reference to informal-settlement and rural areas
service_provider: municipal/regional water and sanitation service (WSS) providers, including SISAR cooperative model; private-sector concessionaires under expanding PPP arrangements
regulatory_model: Brazil's Law 11.445 (2007), the national basic sanitation policy, setting contractual WSS universalization coverage targets (99% water supply, 90% sewage collection/treatment); political-institutional-regulatory (PIR) framework alignment for private-sector participation
population: vulnerable and informal-settlement households lacking water/sanitation access
sample_size: not_applicable (doctrinal/policy analysis drawing on national statistics and documented policy case examples)
effect_measure: descriptive_national_statistics_and_policy_case_examples
effect_estimate: 82% of the Brazilian population had access to WSS in 2019, leaving 40 million people without water access; approximately 100 million Brazilians lack sewage service access and depend on inadequate/rudimentary individual solutions (MDR 2019); 5+ million households occupy more than 13,000 informal settlements (IBGE 2020), a number growing during the COVID-19 pandemic. Law 11.445 sets contractual universalization targets of 99% water supply and 90% sewage collection/treatment coverage. More than R$700 billion ($132 billion) in investment is estimated as needed to reach these targets by 2033. Private-sector-participation/PPP arrangements affect approximately 80% of Brazilian municipalities and over 70% of the population.
source_document: Narzetti & Marques 2022, Water Policy 24(3)
figure: Fig. 1 (Incentives for modeling projects with pro-poor universal WSS coverage)
section: 1. Introduction; 2. Incentives and WSS universalization; 2.2 The Brazilian panorama
exact_location: p.486: 'the process of identifying and recognizing informal areas from the design and the pre-contractual phases improves the legal framework for expanding access to WSS' (ELIGIBILITY/tenure-recognition as precondition for formal service extension). p.488: Law 11.445 established coverage targets (99% water, 90% sewage) to be defined in service contracts; SISAR cooperative model requires an initial subsidy to be replicable across states (hardship_exception/BURDEN). National outcome statistics (82% WSS access, 100 million without sewage) are secondary government/IBGE data, not this study's own primary data collection. record_id R924CF6D8FC56. risk_of_bias_rating deferred per RISK_OF_BIAS.md.

citation: Khan HF, Arshad SA (2022). Beyond water scarcity: Water (in)security and social justice in Karachi. Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies 42, 101140.
subnational_unit: Lyari Township, Southern District, Karachi (11 Union Councils)
service_provider: Karachi Water and Sewerage Board (KWSB), the sole public water utility; informal water vendors, tankers, and collectively-managed building-level supply providers
regulatory_model: post-1970s government regularization of the informal settlement via 90-year household leases enabling inclusion in city water-infrastructure plans; KWSB's self-registration requirement for billing eligibility; official KWSB tariff schedule (e.g., PKR 221 for a 120 sq. yard residential plot)
population: low-income, multi-ethnic households in a semi-regularized informal settlement at the tail-end of the municipal water network
sample_size: 465 household surveys across 11 Union Councils, supplemented by stakeholder interviews (including KWSB officials), participant observation, and water-quality testing of 79 households
tenure_status: semi-regularized (90-year leases granted post-1970s; some households remain non-leased/informal)
legal_status: mixed -- leased/regularized vs. non-leased/informal residences within the same township
effect_measure: descriptive_household_survey_statistics
effect_estimate: 93% of surveyed households (n=465) have piped water connections; all 33 unconnected households fall in the bottom 50th percentile of monthly household income (sample average PKR 22,000; no household earns >=40,000 PKR). Only 16% of households actually rely on KWSB piped supply for day-to-day needs due to intermittency; 77% use two or more water sources. 80% of connected households receive no water bill (67% of these get regular supply); this is attributed by KWSB officials to lack of lease/self-registration or illegal connections. 9% of connected households pay informal collectively-managed-supply charges in addition to formal costs. Households earning <=5,000 PKR/month spend ~18% of monthly income on water vs. ~2% for households earning >=40,000 PKR/month; western Lyari neighborhoods (poorest) spend >20% of income on water. 87% of households reported sewage contamination in piped water; 92.4% of drinking water samples tested positive for Total Coliform (77.2% of these also positive for E. coli).
adjusted_or_unadjusted: unadjusted (descriptive statistics and cross-tabulations by income group)
covariates: household monthly income, water source type, lease/registration status
model_type: mixed-methods (household survey + qualitative interviews/observation + water-quality lab testing)
source_document: Khan & Arshad 2022, Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies 42
figure: Fig. 5 (spatial disparity in % monthly income spent on water), Fig. 7 (water source composition)
section: 2.1 The case study: Lyari Township; 3.1 KWSB performance and billing; 3.2 Alternate sources: household costs and inequities in access
exact_location: p.3: Lyari 'was regularized only after the 1970s, where the new government provided ninety-year leases to households, and allowed Lyari to be considered in the city's water infrastructure plans' (ELIGIBILITY). p.5: 'in order to get billed, the onus is actually on the consumers themselves to visit KWSB's revenue offices and document their connection to the system' -- self-registration BURDEN; officials attribute non-billing among unregistered/non-leased/illegally-connected households to lack of lease or registration (ENFORCEMENT gap enabling free/unbilled use in some cases, while other non-billed households already pay high recurring installation/electricity costs). p.5-6: income-based expenditure disparity in water costs (18% vs. 2% of monthly income).

Documents a real historical ELIGIBILITY mechanism (1970s regularization via 90-year leases as the precondition for inclusion in city water plans) and an ongoing administrative BURDEN (KWSB's self-registration requirement for billing, with lease/registration status determining whether a household is billed, and 'illegal connections' as an enforcement gap). citation: Armstrong A, Hope R, Koehler J (2022). Piped water revenue and investment strategies in rural Africa. Environmental Research: Infrastructure and Sustainability 2, 035003.
subnational_unit: rural piped water schemes across multiple service areas in each country
service_provider: rural piped water scheme operators (public, private, and community-managed arrangements)
regulatory_model: national policies requiring cash tariff contributions from users who can afford it; tariff-setting practices that trade off cost-recovery against political/affordability protections for poor populations; connection-type policy (on-premises vs. off-premises) and payment-method policy (prepaid credit vs. pay-as-you-fetch vs. monthly billing)
population: rural households served (or seeking service) from piped water schemes
sample_size: more than 3,900 monthly operator revenue records, modeled across novel service-area archetypes
effect_measure: GEE_regression_coefficients_on_revenue
effect_estimate: On-premises connections are associated with an average 17% higher tariff level than off-premises connections in 3 of 4 service-area archetypes (GEE regression, controlling for tariff level as a covariate). Off-premises connections with high-dispensing-capacity waterpoints generate the greatest aggregate revenue. Prepaid credit payment is not associated with a revenue advantage over pay-as-you-fetch or monthly billing once tariff level is controlled for. Fewer than 2 in 5 rural African households are estimated to pay for water at all (cited from Banerjee & Morella 2011; Foster & Hope 2017); less than a third of countries fully fund recurring rural water costs from tariff revenue (GLAAS 2019, cited).
extraction_sample_size: >3,900 monthly operator revenue records across Ghana, Rwanda, and Uganda
adjusted_or_unadjusted: adjusted (GEE regression controlling for tariff level and connection/payment-method covariates)
covariates: tariff level, connection type (on/off premises), payment method, waterpoint dispensing capacity
study_design: observational (panel/longitudinal operator revenue records) with descriptive and regression analysis
source_document: Armstrong, Hope & Koehler 2022, Environmental Research: Infrastructure and Sustainability 2
figure: Figure 1 (rural piped water coverage gains 2000-2020), Figure 2 (rural drinking water accessibility)
section: 1. Introduction; 4.2 [connection-type discussion]; 4.3 Revenue from conventional and prepaid credit payments
exact_location: p.14: 'on premises connections are associated with an average 17% higher tariff level' and 'providing water services exclusively on premises poses a potential affordability risk to poorer households who may be unable to afford the up-front or ongoing cash expense associated with higher service charges' (BURDEN/economic_access), pushing them 'to collect lower priced water from informal or unimproved sources'. p.2: cost-recovery tariff-setting goals 'exist in tension with political agendas and tariff strategies that are intended to protect poor populations', and 'poor enforcement is exacerbated by the fact that rural service providers, who are often unpaid volunteers, frequently lack the professional skills to administer appropriate payment rules' (ENFORCEMENT/DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION). p.14-15: standpipes/kiosks 'do not require users to pay connection fees and enable better targeting of subsidies' (hardship_exception).
extraction_note: Rigorous quantitative econometric study (GEE regression on >3,900 monthly operator revenue records across three African countries) modeling how tariff level, connection type, and payment method affect rural piped water revenue and, by direct extension, household affordability and equity. The central BURDEN/economic_access finding -- on-premises connections' 17% tariff premium creating an affordability risk that pushes poorer households toward unimproved/informal sources -- is a genuine calculable regression effect from the study's own operator-level dataset, though the unit of analysis is the service area/operator rather than the individual household, so it is recorded as institutional-level rather than household-level primary data for quantitative-synthesis-eligibility purposes. record_id R746445B4F65D. risk_of_bias_rating deferred per RISK_OF_BIAS.md.

citation: Nicolas-Artero C, Blanco G, Bopp C, Carrasco N (2022). Modes of access to water for domestic use in rural Chile: a typological proposal. Water Policy 24(7), 1179-1196.
subnational_unit: national (rural areas across all regions of Chile), with regional detail (e.g. north vs south) for cistern-truck dependency
service_provider: Rural Drinking Water (APR) Committees/Cooperatives affiliated with the Ministry of Public Works program; "formal" non-APR organizations funded by SUBDERE/MINVU/GORE; "autonomous" self-organized or real-estate-developer-created organizations; urban sanitation concessionaires (for adjacent/peri-urban rural areas)
regulatory_model: Law 20,998 (2019) on Rural Sanitary Services (SSR), regularizing a previously unregulated sector of ~2,558 community water organizations; General Law of Sanitary Services, under which urban sanitation concessionaires are NOT required to deliver water outside their urban concession area, and APR Committees/Cooperatives are similarly not required to supply new rural housing developments; Law on Real-Estate Co-ownership governing water systems as common domain assets in condominiums
population: rural population of Chile (2,257,128 people per CASEN 2017), specifically the 46.3% (just over 1 million) without a networked water supply
sample_size: CASEN 2017 national household survey (nationally/regionally/communally representative); national consolidated database of 2,559 rural water organizations (including 1,961 APR-Program organizations updated June 2020); 5 semi-structured expert interviews (3 Ministry of Public Works officials, 2 APR organization/National Federation leaders)
effect_measure: descriptive typology derived from systematic literature review (12 in-depth papers of 1,107 initially identified) + national survey/administrative-database cross-tabulation
effect_estimate: CASEN (2017): of 2,257,128 rural Chileans, 53.7% are networked; of the remaining 46.3% (>1,000,000 people), 55.6% draw untreated water directly from natural sources, 28.1% are served by APR-Program organizations, 15.8% by non-APR community organizations, 5% other/no answer. Of an estimated 2,559 rural water organizations nationally, 70% are APR-affiliated and 30% are not. Urban sanitation concessionaires' legal non-obligation to serve outside their urban concession area, combined with APR organizations' non-obligation to supply new rural housing developments, is identified as the specific legal mechanism producing 'autonomous' private/developer-created water organizations that lack regularized water rights, land title, tariff systems, or new-user admission criteria -- and the paper documents that some rural/indigenous communities in southern Chile deliberately avoid formalizing under the APR Program specifically to escape state regulatory requirements they consider too burdensome.
extraction_sample_size: CASEN 2017: 2,257,128 rural population (regionally representative); organizational database: 2,559 organizations; 5 expert interviews
adjusted_or_unadjusted: unadjusted (descriptive typology + cross-tabulation of survey/administrative data)
covariates: none (typology-building study; regional stratification only, e.g. north vs. south for cistern-truck dependence)
model_type: mixed-methods typology construction (systematic literature review + quantitative descriptive analysis of national survey and organizational databases + qualitative expert validation)
study_design: mixed-methods: (1) systematic literature review (4 databases, 1,107 initial results narrowed to 12 in-depth papers), (2) quantitative analysis of national household survey (CASEN 2017) and a newly consolidated national database of rural water organizations, (3) semi-structured expert interviews (n=5) to validate the typology
source_document: Nicolas-Artero, Blanco, Bopp & Carrasco 2022, Water Policy 24(7)

extraction_note: Strong, directly analyzed legal-mechanism-to-household-outcome study: a statutory non-obligation to serve (General Law of Sanitary Services) creates a documented gap in legal water-access entitlement for new rural/peri-urban households, driving formation of unregulated 'autonomous' organizations lacking water rights, land title, and tariff/admission systems, and some communities actively avoid legal formalization to escape regulatory burden -- a genuine discretion/accommodation and eligibility dynamic with a household-level access outcome (mode of water access), evidenced with real national survey (CASEN) and organizational-database statistics.

citation: Filčák R, Škobla D (2021). Sanitation Infrastructure at the Systemic Edge: Segregated Roma Settlements and Multiple Health Risks in Slovakia. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 18(11), 6079.
subnational_unit: 22 villages in the Šariš and Spiš historic regions (ethnographic fieldwork sample); national data covers approximately 800 segregated Roma settlements
service_provider: municipal authorities / municipal water and sewerage utilities
regulatory_model: municipal discretion over extension of water/sewerage infrastructure to segregated settlements; Construction Authorities dwelling-registration regime under which non-registered ("illegal") dwellings are used to justify withholding service extension; land tenure/ownership rules (post-communist restitution land partitioning)
population: Roma residents of segregated settlements in Slovakia; approximately 250,000 people nationally (about 5% of national population)
sample_size: 22 villages (small/medium/large settlement strata), 90 semi-structured interviews and group discussions with mayors, municipal administrators, social workers, health authorities, NGOs and Roma residents; national quantitative data from the Atlas of Roma Communities (2019), Office of Public Health Authority disease database, and Ministry of Environment water/sewerage database
effect_measure: descriptive national statistics (Atlas of Roma Communities 2019 cross-tabulated with disease-outbreak database) plus qualitative typology derived from ethnographic fieldwork
effect_estimate: 76% of Roma households on village outskirts have potential access to water pipelines but only 59% are actually connected/using them; 51% have potential access to public sewerage but only 35% are actually connected. Of 4,693 recorded contagious-disease outbreak cases (2014-2018, faecal-oral transmission route, 681 municipalities), 85% occurred in municipalities where at least some Roma households lack water/sewerage connection, 9% in municipalities where ALL Roma households lack sewerage connection, and only 15% in municipalities where Roma households are connected. A three-type typology of municipal governance was derived from fieldwork: Type A (inert/economically disadvantaged, land-ownership/negotiation barriers), Type B (developmental, non-discriminatory, EU-funded improvement), and Type C ('not in my backyard' -- explicitly discriminatory municipalities that use the 'illegal' non-registered status of dwellings and land-tenure issues to justify excluding Roma settlements from sanitation-infrastructure extension while connecting non-Roma dwellings in the same village).
extraction_sample_size: 22 villages, 90 interviews/discussions; national disease dataset 4,693 cases across 681 municipalities (2014-2018); national Atlas of Roma Communities 2019 (~800 settlements, ~250,000 people)
adjusted_or_unadjusted: unadjusted (descriptive cross-tabulation of national administrative datasets; qualitative typology from fieldwork, not a regression model)
covariates: none (descriptive statistics); qualitative typology built from structural variables (sanitation presence, settlement size, development activity, disease incidence) cross-referenced with fieldwork data
model_type: mixed-methods: descriptive cross-tabulation of national datasets + ethnographic qualitative typology construction
study_design: mixed-methods: quantitative desk research on national datasets (Atlas of Roma Communities, disease-outbreak database, water/sewerage database) sequentially informing purposive sampling for qualitative ethnographic fieldwork (semi-structured interviews, group discussions, observation) in 22 villages, January-February 2020
source_document: Filčák & Škobla 2021, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 18(11)
table: Table 1 (research grid: structural variables and fieldwork data by village)
exact_location: p.5: '76% of Roma households... have potential access to water pipelines... only 59%... are actually connected'; p.7: dwellings are 'non-registered by the Construction Authorities' used to justify exclusion; 'Roma dwellings in a settlement are excluded from municipal development with regard to sanitation infrastructure'
extraction_note: Paradigm case for this review's central thesis: documents a real, analyzed municipal-discretion mechanism (a documented three-type typology of local governmentality) under which some municipalities explicitly cite the 'illegal'/non-registered status of Roma dwellings and land-tenure barriers to justify withholding sanitation-infrastructure extension, producing a stark household-level connection gap (76% potential vs 59% actual water access; 51% vs 35% sewerage) strongly correlated with contagious-disease outbreaks. Genuine mixed-methods design combining national administrative-data analysis with ethnographic fieldwork (90 interviews across 22 villages).

citation: Wutich A, Jepson W, Velasco C, Roque A, Gu Z, Hanemann M, Hossain MJ, Landes L, Larson R, Li WW, Morales-Pate O, Patwoary N, Porter S, Tsai Y-S, Zheng M, Westerhoff P (2022). Water insecurity in the Global North: A review of experiences in U.S. colonias communities along the Mexico border. WIREs Water 9(4), e1595.
subnational_unit: colonias in the four U.S.-Mexico border states: Texas (1,800+ colonias), New Mexico (154), Arizona (104), California (35)
service_provider: municipal water utilities (where annexed); private/informal well systems and small water systems (where unannexed)
regulatory_model: municipal annexation law and 'municipal underbounding' (intentional non-annexation of low-income minority unincorporated communities via boundary gerrymandering); historical Texas 'contract for deed' property-sale law (legal until 1995, no service-provision obligation on developers until a 1989 Texas law change); federal Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA, 40 U.S.C. section 300f et seq.) size-based regulatory classification (systems serving fewer than 3,300 people face lighter monitoring/reporting requirements; private wells largely unregulated)
population: colonias residents along the U.S.-Mexico border, predominately Mexican and Central American immigrant agricultural/informal-economy workers; estimated 1 million people
sample_size: secondary narrative/focused review synthesizing the published colonias water-insecurity literature (no primary sample of its own)
effect_measure: narrative synthesis of the published empirical/legal literature on U.S. colonias water insecurity (secondary review; no independently generated effect estimate)
effect_estimate: Synthesizes literature documenting: municipal 'selective underbounding' (intentional non-annexation of colonias via 'conspicuous gerrymandering' of municipal boundaries) that excludes colonias from municipal water/sewer systems, driven by low expected tax revenue relative to infrastructure cost; the cost of remaining unannexed ranges from several million dollars for a 100-resident colonia to $20 million for a colonia with thousands of residents; historical Texas 'contract for deed' land-sale arrangements (unrecorded/informal, single-default forfeiture) that left developers under no legal obligation to provide water/sanitation until a 1989 Texas law change; SDWA's size-based regulatory threshold (fewer than 3,300 people served) resulting in infrequent water-quality monitoring for many colonias systems, and private wells (common in colonias) falling outside SDWA coverage entirely with generally no water-quality monitoring at all.

covariates: not_applicable

risk_of_bias_tool: AMSTAR 2 (secondary systematic review) / not applicable as primary-study tool

section: 6.2 Municipal underbounding in U.S. colonias; 6.3 Failures in water quality monitoring in U.S. colonias

citation: Saker A, Bernal Pedraza A, Narayan AS (2022). Regulating Citywide Inclusive Sanitation (CWIS) in Colombia. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 19(9), 5669.
subnational_unit: national regulatory framework, with reference to municipal-level implementation (informal settlements, high-risk zones, peri-urban underserved areas)
service_provider: public water/sanitation utilities and small/community service providers regulated under Colombia's public-utilities framework
regulatory_model: Law 142-1994 (public utilities services law, sewered-only sanitation definition); Decree 1272-2017 and Water Regulatory Authority (WRA) Resolution 699-2021 (flexible tariff/service scheme for underserved areas, no obligation to expand to non-formalized zones, requires municipal certification of 'urbanization prospect'); Law 2044-2020 (obliges local authorities to address informal-settlement vulnerability via service provision or relocation); Law 388-1997 (bars public-service provision in high-risk zones, no interim solution pending relocation); national funding requirement of land-legality certification for WSS projects; environmental permitting regime (AECs) for onsite sanitation infrastructure
population: households in informal settlements, high-risk zones, and underserved peri-urban areas of Colombian cities lacking sewered sanitation access
sample_size: qualitative case study: in-depth policy review of Colombian laws/decrees/resolutions/court rulings plus semi-structured interviews and workshops with key stakeholders in the urban sanitation sector (national and local government representatives, regulators, utilities, practitioners)
effect_measure: qualitative thematic analysis of policy documents and stakeholder interviews/workshops, with descriptive statistics cited from national sources (e.g., percentage of outdated land-planning instruments)
effect_estimate: Identifies specific, analyzed regulatory barriers to informal/underserved-area sanitation access: (1) ELIGIBILITY -- subsidies for WSS costs apply only to sewered service-provision schemes, so households relying on non-sewered technologies (the CWIS-eligible population) are not eligible for financial assistance; funding for WSS projects nationally requires certification of land legality, barring informal settlements without resolved property status from national funds. (2) DISCRETION -- expansion to 'non formalized zones' requires a signed municipal commitment that the zone has 'urbanization prospect,' which 'is not always within the mayor's interest,' making service delivery in informal settlements highly dependent on the mayor's political will; 88% of municipal land-planning instruments are outdated or inaccurate, leaving marginalized zones outside formal planning tools. (3) ENFORCEMENT/EXCLUSION -- Law 388-1997 prohibits providing public services in high-risk zones with no interim/temporary solution while (often lengthy) relocation is pending, and legal ambiguity about implementing any development in high-risk zones leads utilities to avoid these areas to escape control-entity sanctions. (4) PROCEDURAL/DELAY -- environmental discharge permits for onsite sanitation (e.g., septic tank ground-discharge permits) can take over a year to approve, at times exceeding the cost of the facility itself; Resolution 699-2021 is 59 pages and 'too complex for community or small service providers to understand and apply.'
extraction_sample_size: qualitative case study: national policy/legal document review + semi-structured interviews and workshops with key sanitation-sector stakeholders
covariates: not_applicable
model_type: qualitative thematic analysis of policy documents and stakeholder consultation
study_design: descriptive qualitative case study: in-depth policy/legal review (laws, decrees, resolutions, court rulings) combined with semi-structured interviews and stakeholder workshops
source_document: Saker, Bernal Pedraza & Narayan 2022, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 19(9)
table: Table 4 (summary of barriers to CWIS identified through stakeholder consultation)
section: 3. Results (Service Delivery; Land Management; Environmental; Financial subsections)

extraction_note: Exceptionally rich, directly analyzed multi-mechanism case study matching this review's core thesis: identifies eligibility (sewered-only subsidy scheme), documentation/tenure (land-legality certification for funding), discretion (mayoral political will over zone formalization), and enforcement/exclusion (high-risk-zone service prohibition with no interim alternative) mechanisms all producing household/community-level sanitation-access exclusion in Colombian informal settlements. Real qualitative empirical methodology (policy review + interviews + workshops), not doctrinal argument alone.

citation: Dasgupta S, Agarwal N (2022). Experimenting with Urban-Rural Partnerships for Sustainable Sanitation in India: Learning from Practice. Land 11(7), 1021.
subnational_unit: Dhenkanal district, Odisha (Dhenkanal municipality and neighbouring gram panchayats/rural local governments)
service_provider: Dhenkanal urban local body (municipal faecal sludge management/FSM system) extending service to rural gram panchayats via an intergovernmental partnership
regulatory_model: Informal, market-led pre-pilot arrangement (higher rural service charge, no formal agreement); pilot formal cooperative agreement between the urban local body and gram panchayats (explicitly 'an agreement and not a contract,' lacking equivalent legal enforceability); jurisdictional service-area eligibility determined by distance thresholds and non-contiguous gram panchayat geography; 2021 national government letter (S-18011/6/2021-SBM-DDWS) recommending urban local governments extend services to neighbouring gram panchayats under Swachh Bharat Mission phase 2
population: rural households in gram panchayats surrounding Dhenkanal municipality relying on on-site sanitation systems (septic tanks, single/twin pits) requiring faecal sludge management
sample_size: 1,000-household rural survey; structured interviews with sarpanchs (elected heads) of 8 rural local governments; FSTP capacity/utilization transactional records (2019-2020); Census of India 2011 demographic data
effect_measure: descriptive statistics from household survey, FSTP utilization records, and financial/tariff records; qualitative practice-research observation
effect_estimate: Before the pilot, an informal market-led arrangement charged rural households 1.5-2 times the per-trip service fee paid by urban households; rural households constituted 13% of all households served by the Dhenkanal FSTP (Jan 2019-Feb 2020), which had approximately 50% spare daily capacity (27 kilolitre/day capacity). Following formalization of the urban-rural partnership, service charges for rural households were reduced, and institutional responsibilities were clarified. Jurisdictional eligibility was constrained by an approximately 10km distance threshold from the urban FSTP, complicated by gram panchayats' non-contiguous village/hamlet geography, creating the risk of 'institutionally sanctioned unequal access to services' among villages within the same jurisdiction depending on which side of the threshold they fell.
extraction_sample_size: 1,000 rural households surveyed; 8 gram panchayat sarpanch interviews; FSTP transactional records 2019-2020
adjusted_or_unadjusted: unadjusted (descriptive statistics; practice-research/action-research design, not a regression model)
covariates: none (descriptive analysis of survey, FSTP capacity/utilization, and financial data)
model_type: participatory action/practice research with descriptive quantitative analysis (household survey, FSTP capacity-demand matching) and qualitative process documentation
study_design: participatory action research: authors directly supported design and implementation (2019-2021) of India's first intergovernmental urban-rural sanitation partnership, combining a 1,000-household survey, sarpanch interviews, and secondary administrative/geospatial data
source_document: Dasgupta & Agarwal 2022, Land 11(7)
figure: Figure 6 (types of systems emptied, rural vs urban); Figure 7 (non-contiguous gram panchayat geography example)
section: 4. Results (4.1 Planning; 4.2/4.3 Service Delivery and Institutional Arrangements)
exact_location: p.8: 'rural households constituted 13% of all households served'; p.9: 'the gram panchayats could find explaining the resulting institutionally sanctioned unequal access to services difficult to justify'; p.14 (later section): 'as an agreement and not a contract, in its current form, it does not equip gram panchayats' with enforceable standing
extraction_note: Participatory action-research case study of India's first intergovernmental urban-rural sanitation partnership. Genuine eligibility/service-area mechanism: jurisdictional distance thresholds and non-contiguous gram panchayat geography create a documented risk of unequal within-jurisdiction access; the cooperative agreement's weaker-than-contract legal status is explicitly flagged by the authors as a governance risk. Real household-level affordability outcome (rural service-charge reduction) and service-coverage outcome (13% rural share of FSTP service).

citation: Dugard J (2021). Water Rights in a Time of Fragility: An Exploration of Contestation and Discourse around Cape Town's 'Day Zero' Water Crisis. Water 13(22), 3247.
subnational_unit: national (South African courts) with focus on Cape Town water crisis (Aug 2017-June 2018) and prior Johannesburg (Soweto/Phiri), Durban, Ekurhuleni, and KwaZulu-Natal cases
service_provider: municipal water services authorities (a local government mandate in South Africa)
regulatory_model: South African Constitution section 27(1)(b) (justiciable right to water); prepaid water meters imposed on poor households that automatically disconnect supply once the monthly Free Basic Water allocation is exhausted; indigent-registration requirement to access subsidized/free water tariffs; case law: Mazibuko and Others v City of Johannesburg (2009, Constitutional Court -- unsuccessful challenge to prepayment meters/automatic disconnection and FBW adequacy); Manqele v Durban Transitional Metropolitan Council (2001, unsuccessful sufficiency challenge); Residents of Bon Vista Mansions v Southern Metropolitan Local Council (2001, disconnection without notice/process is a prima facie constitutional violation); Mtungwa and Others v Ekurhuleni Metropolitan Municipality (2011, ordered provision of basic water/sanitation to informal settlements); The Federation for Sustainable Environment v Minister of Water Affairs (2012, ordered potable water within 72 hours after acid-mine-drainage contamination); Mshengu and Others v Msunduzi Local Municipality (2019, established state duty to provide water across private land to farm-dwellers)
population: impoverished South African households, particularly in Soweto/Phiri (Johannesburg), informal settlements, townships, and farm-dweller communities
sample_size: qualitative empirical-legal research: interviews with water rights activists and lawyers over a 3-year review period (July 2017-July 2020), plus systematic review of water-rights case law (74 total socio-economic-rights Constitutional Court cases 1994-2020, of which only 1 concerned the right to water; 6 total water-rights cases across all courts) and secondary consumption/service-access statistics
effect_measure: legal-empirical case analysis (systematic review of case law and interviews) combined with cited national household-access statistics
effect_estimate: In 2016, 89.9% of South African households had access to piped water (44.4% inside the dwelling, 30% inside the yard, 1.9% from a neighbour, 13.5% from a communal tap), up from 67% in 1994 (33% of the population, ~12 million people, lacked adequate access). Despite this, rural municipalities and informal-settlement/farm-dwelling households continue to experience water-services backlogs, disconnections, and unsafe drinking water; many low/no-income households cannot afford tariffs beyond the Free Basic Water allocation, which typically requires 'undignified registration as an indigent' to access (a documentation/eligibility barrier) and is often inadequate for multi-dwelling households. Only 1 of 74 Constitutional Court socio-economic-rights cases (1994-2020) concerned the right to water (Mazibuko, unsuccessful for the applicants), versus 24 property-rights, 23 housing-rights, and 10 land-rights cases -- a striking under-litigation of water rights relative to other socio-economic rights despite documented ongoing water insecurity.
extraction_sample_size: interviews with water rights activists/lawyers over a 3-year period; systematic case-law review (74 Constitutional Court socio-economic-rights cases, 6 water-rights cases across all South African courts)
covariates: not_applicable
model_type: qualitative legal-empirical research: systematic case-law analysis plus semi-structured interviews with legal/activist stakeholders
study_design: descriptive qualitative case study combining doctrinal/case-law analysis with empirical interview data (water rights activists and lawyers, South Africa, 2017-2020 review period), authored by a law professor
source_document: Dugard 2021, Water 13(22)
section: 1.1 The Curious Case of the Relative Absence of Water Rights Contestation in South Africa; 1.1.1
exact_location: p.3: 'Mazibuko was an unsuccessful legal challenge by impoverished Soweto residents against the imposition of prepayment water meters, which automatically disconnected their water supply following the exhaustion of the inadequate Free Basic Water amount'; p.4: 'many low-income and no-income households are unable to afford water tariffs beyond the Free Basic Water amount... typically entails undignified registration as an indigent'
extraction_note: Directly on this review's enforcement/disconnection and eligibility/documentation mechanism families: prepaid meters that auto-disconnect once a Free Basic Water allocation is exhausted (ENFORCEMENT), and an indigent-registration requirement to access that allocation (DOCUMENTATION/ELIGIBILITY). Real household-level outcomes (piped-water access disaggregated by connection type) and a systematic count of water-rights litigation (1 of 74 relevant Constitutional Court cases) demonstrating under-enforcement of the constitutional right to water via courts despite the mechanism's continued operation.

citation: Huston A, Gaskin S, Moriarty P, Watsisi M (2021). More Sustainable Systems Through Consolidation? The Changing Landscape of Rural Drinking Water Service Delivery in Uganda. Water Alternatives 14(1), 248-270.
service_provider: National Water and Sewerage Corporation (national utility), regional Umbrella utilities (established 2016), and community-managed point-source structures
regulatory_model: Uganda Ministry of Water and Environment (MWE) sector guidelines, policy, and monitoring frameworks; national consolidation strategy transitioning from community-managed point sources to professional piped utilities; area service provision/performance-contract models (proposed CBMS+); tariff-setting and enforcement authority differing by institutional model; unclear service-authority hierarchy between District Local Governments and utilities
population: rural households in Kabarole District relying on community-managed water points or newly-extending utility piped networks
sample_size: household and infrastructure surveys, management assessment, key informant interviews (including 4 National Water managers), and stakeholder workshops (2017-2019)
effect_measure: descriptive statistics from household/infrastructure surveys and management assessment; comparative institutional analysis of service delivery models
effect_estimate: The two utility models (National Water and regional Umbrella) outperformed community management, which had less than 20% of community management structures operational at water points. National Water 'has the technical capacity to enforce payment by cutting off supply in response to non-payment,' while the newer Umbrella utility and community management structures lack this authority/capacity; only utilities consistently enforce tariff payment. In 2019, an estimated 38% of households reported paying for water regularly (about half within Fort Portal municipality, served by National Water) and 28% reported making ad hoc post-breakdown contributions. Tariffs per 20L varied by provider: 25 UGX (National Water subsidised public standposts) to 94 UGX (Umbrella domestic connections). All 4 National Water managers interviewed reported high effective household demand for new paid connections, including in areas previously served by free lower-service-level water.
extraction_sample_size: household and infrastructure surveys across multiple service models in Kabarole District; management assessment; key informant interviews (4 National Water managers plus Umbrella/community managers); stakeholder workshops
adjusted_or_unadjusted: unadjusted (descriptive comparative statistics across service delivery models)
covariates: none (descriptive cross-model comparison using a systems/sustainability building-blocks framework)
model_type: mixed-methods systems-approach comparative case study (sustainability building blocks framework)
study_design: mixed-methods case study comparing rural drinking water service delivery models (community management vs. two utility models) via household/infrastructure surveys, management assessment, key informant interviews, and stakeholder workshops, 2017-2019
source_document: Huston, Gaskin, Moriarty & Watsisi 2021, Water Alternatives 14(1)
exact_location: p.262: National Water 'has the technical capacity to enforce payment by cutting off supply in response to non-payment, which forces out non-paying customers'; p.262: 'an estimated 38% of households reported paying for water regularly'

effect_estimate: Of 56 water-management groups with complete data: 25 (44.6%) used proportional-equality payment (fee scaled to livestock owned), 7 (12.5%) an attenuated proportional form, and 24 (42.9%) numerical equality (flat fee per household regardless of usage). Active state/NGO involvement (regular visits, on-site presence) was significantly associated with communities adopting proportional equality (phi = -0.478, P = 0.000); without active state involvement, three intra-community dynamics (administration/counting costs, wealth/bargaining power of large herd-owners, and multiplex kinship-based sharing norms) pushed communities toward numerical equality instead. Proportional equality was significantly associated with higher satisfaction/success on every indicator measured: satisfaction with the institutional rules themselves (rank-biserial correlation rbc = 0.559, P = 0.000), with water point committee work (rbc = 0.427, P = 0.017), with community cooperation (rbc = 0.406, P = 0.006), and with general water-management satisfaction (rbc = 0.389, P = 0.003). No significant association was found between the payment rule and the technological infrastructure's susceptibility to failure (phi = -0.01, n.s.), suggesting the satisfaction effect is social/institutional rather than a proxy for better-performing boreholes. An agent-based simulation (calibrated on 80 households' actual livestock distribution; Gini = 0.49 for livestock ownership) projected that under numerical equality (flat fee, all pay the same regardless of usage), a rich household's share of total water usage rose from an already-disproportionate baseline to about 18 times a poor household's share after 100 months, while the livestock-ownership Gini coefficient rose further over the same period -- i.e., poor and moderately-well-off households' flat payments effectively subsidize both the current water consumption and the future wealth accumulation of richer households under the numerical-equality regime.

effect_estimate: Despite sustained institutional intervention and infrastructure investment by AyA and the Ministry of Health in Amubri between 1990 and 2022, deficiencies in drinking-water access, quality, and system sustainability persisted throughout the period. State management was marked by lack of project continuity, budgetary and technical limitations, community conflicts, and weak local appropriation ('apropiación') of the aqueduct systems built by the state. A centralized, technical-administrative approach to water governance -- applying national regulatory/sanitary criteria without adequate negotiation, intercultural openness, or adaptation to local Bribri organizational practices and economic conditions -- is identified as the central mechanism behind the persistence of potability/sustainability problems despite investment. Cultural resistance to water chlorination and divergent local perceptions of contamination further reflect a disarticulation between institutional technical frameworks and Bribri sociocultural understandings of the resource. The study concludes that policy effectiveness has been limited by this centralized, culturally-insensitive approach, and calls for a participatory, intercultural water-management model to make the human right to water effective for the Amubri community.

service_provider: UDUMA (professional service delivery company, affermage/lease contract)
regulatory_model: Mali's Water Act (2002) defines municipalities as service authorities for rural water supply (Art. 49-50) that must delegate service provision via formal contract (Art. 51) to a private/public entity or legally recognized water user association (Art. 45)
population: 30 municipalities in Sikasso region contracting UDUMA for rural drinking water service delivery covering existing community hand pumps
sample_size: Qualitative case study: contracting documents, interviews, and field reports (exact interview count not numerically stated)
effect_measure: qualitative case-study description (contract theory analysis)
effect_estimate: Under the affermage contract (Nov. 2018, 15-year duration), 30 municipalities granted UDUMA the exclusive right to operate all existing community hand pumps and collect user tariffs (full cost recovery), in exchange for infrastructure rehabilitation investment and a 3% annual turnover fee to local governments plus bi-annual reporting. Despite meeting contracted service-delivery obligations, UDUMA consistently missed revenue targets because the contract is 'incomplete': it cannot enforce local water demand (the non-exclusive nature of rural water sources means households retain autonomy to use alternative/seasonal sources, and there is limited ability of rural users to pay). Contract renegotiation -- involving both original parties' agreement and the mobilization of external actors and capital -- was found to be the mechanism through which service providers and authorities addressed this incompleteness, but renegotiation itself is conditional and not guaranteed to succeed, given the wider institutional environment's limited enforcement capacity.

effect_estimate: Despite nearly a decade of dedicated federal funding strategies (First Nations Water Management Strategy 2003; First Nations Water and Wastewater Action Plan 2008), the National Assessment of First Nations Water and Wastewater Systems (2011) found 1,880 homes in Canada still lacked in-house piped water in 2009, and average drinking water advisories (DWAs) in First Nations communities rose to 123/year over 2003-2007. The authors conclude that social groups with lesser capacity to defend their interests (poor residents of peripheral metropolitan districts) are structurally more vulnerable to this institutionally-produced hydrosocial scarcity, independent of, and potentially aggravated by, climatic/bulk-water-availability stressors.

effect_estimate: The study traces Brazil's first sanitation and water-resource public policies from the Portuguese colonial period to the 1930s, showing that water regulation before the 19th century served primarily to facilitate economic extraction (sesmaria land/water grants for sugar-mill and mining operations) rather than public water-access provision. From the 18th-19th centuries, public fountains (chafarizes) -- financed through taxes on wine and cachaca plus judicial revenues, exemplified by Rio de Janeiro's Aqueduto da Carioca (completed 1750) -- provided nominally free and open community water access in colonial cities (Rio de Janeiro, Vila Rica, Salvador, Recife), but the actual transport of water from fountain to residence, and the collection/disposal of household excreta, was performed by enslaved people ('tigres'), meaning that practical, convenient in-home water access remained conditioned on the economic capacity to own or hire enslaved labor. The authors interpret this pattern, and Brazil's broader historical trajectory of centralized/fragmented, externally-dependent water-and-sanitation policy formation, through a dependency-theory lens emphasizing the country's structurally subordinate position in the international economic system as a persistent constraint shaping domestic sanitation institution-building.
